doc.title: Arturo O'Farrill interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 6, 2024

title: European melody and Duke Ellington's melodicism
summary: Asked about melody and form, he cites European melodicism and chromatic harmony and praises Ellington's melodies as classical in stature.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Were there certain parts of the world where, let’s say the melodic contributions came from? We’ve been talking mostly about rhythm. What about the melody and the form?

Without a doubt much of the information that we have in the thing we call jazz comes from European melodicism. It comes from the chromatic, you know chromatic harmony. So in some ways this is funny that you said that because I was just listening to “Isfahan” © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

and I was just again — I was listening to “Isfahan” and “Warm Valley” and I was thinking about one of the greatest gifts of music is Duke Ellington’s sense of melodicism. Just the pacing and the outlaying of a Duke Ellington melody, to me, is as elegant as anything that Beethoven wrote and I’m a classically trained musician. My degrees are in classical music. But when I listen to Duke Ellington I can’t help but think this is classical music. It’s — you don’t have to dress it up. It’s already arrived fully formed and as eloquent as any — as eloquent as any Beethoven piano sonata. It’s just — you know — so yeah melodically I think the best — when good — and I’m going to say this again, it’s not a black or white thing. When musicians embrace aesthetics that are forged in Mother Africa and that are brought forth through the crucible of European harmony and performance practice, these things come together in a way that to me feels global. It to me feels global. And then you realize that after this thing has been born its best expression comes throughout the world — incredible musicians in Europe and Asia and practitioners of this craft at the highest levels who are all over the world, and you realize that the word “global jazz” is talking not only about the beginnings, the contemporary moments of jazz, but also the future of this music. And it’s funny because it, to me, it’s like — it is very important to understand the migratory power of music. Music is the ultimate migratory power. When we listen to a piece of music we have to recognize that it comes through a place but it comes from many sources.
